text: जाओ किसी कॉन्फ़्रेंस में — ज्ञान बहुत देंगे, जो नहीं आते ऐसी बैठकों में वो बहुत कम मिलेंगे।
अरे, पर बातें भी तो ज़रूरी हैं, हम नहीं करेंगे तो कौन करेगा?
जिनकी बातें हैं, वो करेंगे — एक नहीं, कई हज़ार हैं, और ना वैसा मंच है, ना उनके लिए कोई बाज़ार है।
ग़रीब गंजा ही रह जाता है, अमीर बुढ़ापे में भी नए बाल लगवाता है।
मैं भी बातें बहुत करता हूँ — काम, उससे भी कम। बाल मेरे भी नहीं हैं, और मिज़ाज सूरज से भी गरम।
किसे बुलाना कहाँ बुलाना, कोई रुपया कोई आना। किसे बुलाना क्यों बुलाना, उसने अब नहीं आना।
इधर हुआ जो उधर कहाँ है? नीचे क्यों ये आसमान है? शौक गया है सांस गयी है, मन की आवाज गयी है।
किसे बताना क्यों बताना, सब सही जब यही सुनाना। उधर की बातें नहीं बताना, इधर नहीं हुआ जब आना।
धीमे धीमे यूंही रोजाना, वक्त कटे दिन घटे, दर्द जब नहीं बंटे, कल शायद आसमान हटे।
धीरे धीरे थम गया, वक्त सारा कहाँ गया? ना जाने कब ये आसमान हटेगा, दर्द मेरा कब घटेगा?
लोग बात बहुत करते हैं, मौका मिलते ही बातें चालू।
काम का बना दिया है हलवा, और बातों का है असीम जलवा।
मुद्दा सामने ही था, लेकिन पहले ज़रा किस्से-कहानी हो जाए।
तस्वीरें छोटी होनी चाहिए, लोग पास आकर देखते हैं।
दूर से तो चाँद भी दिखता है, पर उसका रोज़ थोड़ी सोचते हैं।
वो बड़ा है, यूँ ही खड़ा है, उसे ख़ास थोड़ी समझते हैं।
वो तस्वीर जो छोटी होती है, उसमें तुझे खोजते हैं।
मेरी एक तस्वीर बनाना, उसमें छोटी-सी एक लकीर बनाना।
लकीर के इस तरफ़ मुझे बनाना, और उस तरफ़ रखना ज़माना।
इसलिए अब नहीं बुलाना, नहीं बुलाना, नहीं बुलाना।
Believe me there are people who are only drinking a litre of water everyday.

text: I am talking about some of the folks who are part of Rural India Youth Leadership program.
These spaces, or clubs, are run by a youth formally called a youth mobiliser, whose presence ensures the smooth running of these clubs.
Each youth mobiliser manages two separate clubs in their respective panchayats.
The members are youth volunteers, who engage in these clubs for a year, and through various activities, they learn leadership and active citizenship.
To understand the motivation behind this, it's essential to look at the system itself and how these club spaces function.
Understanding the system behind these spaces is crucial to realising the motivation in rural leadership programs.
A Youth Mobiliser running these clubs is supported by Youth Coordinators, each of whom work with 4-5 Youth Mobilisers.
Each Youth Mobiliser is responsible for two club spaces, facilitating bi-weekly meetings.
The youth mobilisers plan sessions, share information, and collaborate, creating a network of knowledge exchange.
The system fosters an environment of support, learning, and collective growth.
In some panchayats, there is a lack of comfortable areas, and hence, some of these clubs exist in spaces like the one mentioned at the start of this blog.
The thought that they can become leaders of their own lives and, in turn, make their communities’ lives easier?
It’s a place where they can just play one day and discuss serious topics like gender equality and inclusion on another.
Why are they sitting without complaining about the heat, while many of us in urban spaces struggle to function without air conditioning?
For many, it seems the idea of togetherness is stronger than the discomfort of physical conditions.
When it comes to learning spaces everyone has different notions as well.
How people perceive these spaces and how they see themselves being present in that space has a huge impact.
Their complaints, if any, are more about personal schedules clashing with the club sessions.
Despite this, they express a strong sense of love for the club and the space itself.
Many even say things like “हमारा क्लब” (our club) and “मेरा क्लब” (my club), showing how they’ve developed a sense of ownership.
Not just spaces but even people around whom I feel stressed.
How can I learn from the volunteers and make sure that I also have at least a percentage of the resilience that these folks have?
It's still a long way for me to go in this regard but this event definitely struck a chord in me.
I still wonder what goes through their minds, and how they ensure their own learning in spaces that can hinder functioning.
It creates a powerful connection, turning even the most uncomfortable spaces into something better than an air-conditioned room.
The love for being part of something bigger and the desire to learn, grow, and share with others shine through.
Perhaps, it’s not just about leadership or emotional exchange, but the simple, powerful act of coming together in a space that feels like their own.
This profound sense of togetherness is key to understanding motivation in rural leadership programs.
It was a choice I made, though I precisely don’t remember when.
What I do remember is faith slowly being overtaken by a thought process that made it difficult for me to be a theist.

It was the only time it mattered — and the only time it didn’t.
Not because we had to, but because it felt proportionate — small stakes for something that wasn’t supposed to matter.
Five of us, one deck, and evenings that stretched without resistance, as if time itself had agreed to wait.
The kind of space that absorbed noise and never returned it.
The unfinished sentences that found their way back to the table, disguised as jokes.
Even in conversation, there was a subtle pull; people adjusted around him without noticing.
The cards remained indifferent — to confidence, to timing, to certainty.
“You’re remembering too much,” Kabir said once, watching him shuffle.
“You’re not remembering enough.” Kabir held his gaze a second longer than usual.
Once, with a full house — beaten by a royal flush he didn’t see coming.
Just stared at the table, fingers resting near his cards, as if recalculating something larger than the hand.
Later that night, when the others were talking, he said quietly — “I shouldn’t miss that.” No one answered.
“You played that wrong.” “That was predictable.” “You’re overvaluing pairs.” He said it lightly.
“Why does it matter?” Aarav asked once, after the others had left.
Even the apartment felt temporary — already in the process of becoming memory.
The city outside was unusually clear, lights stretching farther than they should.
It had always been part of the rhythm — when the room felt too full, we stepped outside.
“Predictable,” Dev said, stacking chips with deliberate precision.
Not because there was no tension — but because Kabir never offered resistance in a form Dev could engage with.
“And you don’t enough.” A flicker crossed Dev’s face — brief, uncontained.
“Four years of this — and you thought — ” “Dev,” Aarav said quietly.
A card near the edge lifted in the wind, trembled, then settled back into place.
Aarav kept looking at the space Dev had occupied, as if absence might reverse itself.
When someone else did, he would sit for a while, watch a few hands, then leave early.
